source: Tetzlaff, Simonsmeier, Peters and Brod (2025) A cornerstone of adaptivity: a meta-analysis of the expertise reversal effect (full text, CC BY, pedocs copy)
finding: Verified from the full text. Abstract numbers match the earlier snippet: low prior knowledge gains from high assistance, high prior knowledge gains from low assistance, and the first side is larger.
numbers: 60 experimental studies, 176 effect sizes (88 per prior-knowledge level), N=5924, 35 journals, 1992-2024, sample sizes 17 to 357 (median 73). Low-PK: d=0.505, 95% CI [0.260, 0.750], k=88, j=60, Q(87)=475.233, I2=90.87%. High-PK: d=-0.428, CI [-0.647, -0.209], Q(88)=284.457, I2=87.55%. Difference of differences: d=0.971, CI [0.631, 1.312]. Searches in PsycINFO and ERIC (Dec 2022, Nov 2024), PRISMA, metafor with clubSandwich robust errors.
quote: Low Prior knowledge learners learn better from high-assistance instruction (d = 0.505).
limits: Heterogeneity is very high on both sides (I2 about 88 to 91%), so the mean is not a good guide to any one setting. The authors call 0.971 a strong effect but say it is lower than the 1.72 in Kalyuga 2007 and explain this by weighting, sample size and clustering. No moderator test on the difference of differences. Data only on request.
agent_relevance: Plan for a lesson effect of about +0.5 on weak classes and about -0.4 on strong classes, with huge spread. Do not plan on 1.7.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) publication bias, inclusion rules and screening (full text)
finding: Publication bias tests found nothing. Inclusion required random assignment to instructional designs and a domain-specific prior-knowledge measure; general intelligence did not count unless a domain test was also present.
numbers: Egger tests not significant: low-PK z=0.568, p=.57; high-PK z=0.299, p=.77. Trim-and-fill funnel plots shown (Figs 2 and 3). Screening: 1589 unique records, 1440 screened, 279 full-text, main exclusions: no domain knowledge measure n=65, no variation in design n=52, missing data n=32. Kappa for inclusion 0.85; coding agreement 94.63%. 23 authors (62%) answered the data request, 3 supplied data.
limits: Only published databases searched (PsycINFO, ERIC); the authors themselves suggest a community call for unpublished work. Egger tests on 88 correlated effects per side have low power. Moderator cells often have 2 to 8 studies.
agent_relevance: Closes the worry that the reversal literature is only a file drawer, but only weakly: the funnel test is weak and grey literature was not searched.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) moderators: educational status, content area, how prior knowledge was assessed (Tables 1 to 3)
finding: Effect sizes depend on how experts were defined and who was studied. Moderator tables are printed as contrasts to a reference level and the text extraction of the tables is partly garbled, so only the clear cells are used here.
numbers: Educational status moderated both sides (low-PK R2=25.92%, high-PK R2=8.47%). Low-PK effect: primary school about -0.29 (j=2, k=4, CI [-0.84, 0.27]), secondary 0.70 (j=3), vocational 0.63, higher education 0.99 [0.34, 1.63] (j=18, k=27), studies comparing groups of several statuses 1.05. Content area moderated low-PK (R2=20.59%): crafts, law and business (coded other) 1.24 [0.42, 2.05] (j=6); humanities and language about 1.08 lower than that reference, weak. Content area did not moderate high-PK. Assessment of prior knowledge moderated high-PK (R2=50.00%): grade-level definition -0.95 [-1.32, -0.58] (j=8, k=13) as reference; measured and dichotomised knowledge about 0.74 higher than the reference (implied roughly -0.21, my arithmetic, not printed), intervention-induced about 0.75 higher, profession or field of study -0.08 relative. Low-PK assessment moderator not significant.
quote: Defining prior knowledge levels via measurement and then dichotomizing is also likely to create smaller average differences between groups.
limits: Confounded: education level, domain and assessment type overlap. Few studies per cell. Contrast coding makes printed numbers easy to misread. The implied -0.21 is derived by the reviewer, not stated by the authors.
agent_relevance: The closest analogue for an agent is measured, dichotomised competence in one domain. That is the weakest-reversal case (roughly -0.2). Large reversals come from comparing groups that differ a lot (novice vs professional). A within-model split by pass rate should expect a small negative side.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) discussion: asymmetry, limitations and advice
finding: The authors say the reversal is not symmetric: giving help to novices matters more than withholding it from experts. They name dichotomising two continuous variables as the likely reason for the huge heterogeneity. They recommend repeated assessment of knowledge as it grows and gradual fading.
numbers: Ordinal pattern: even where low assistance won for both groups, the gap was larger for low-PK. Weaker evidence in primary school and in humanities and language learning; two explanations given, element interactivity of the tasks and accumulated expertise, with educational status partly confounded with age.
quote: Independent of the mechanism that can be used to explain this asymmetry, the instructional implication is to rather provide assistance than to withhold it when in doubt.
limits: The meta-analysis cannot choose between theories (stated limitation). It does not test fading directly. Footnote: an ordinal interaction becomes disordinal only outside the observed range of prior knowledge.
agent_relevance: Default rule for S0: when unsure about a class, show the lesson. Withhold only where measured pass rate is clearly high. In human data, showing a redundant lesson costs less than hiding a needed one.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench v4, Appendix D.6.1 trajectory audit of self-generated skills
finding: Bears on gap 9 and gap 7. Self-written skills fail for four reasons: the solver often never opens them, authoring uses up the trial, confident wrong gotchas become load-bearing, and the one clear win was answer leakage.
numbers: Audit of 12 trajectories over 10 task-configuration pairs. In the pre-baked Codex and Gemini CLI family, 10 of 12 audited trajectories never listed, read or mentioned the generated skills. threejs-to-obj: creator and solver shared one context, creator work used up the trial, both baselines passed. 3d-scan-calc: generated pack hard-coded a 1000x unit conversion, both solver trials ran it unquestioned, mass off by three orders of magnitude (verifier patched 10 days later to also accept mm, so some zeros are artefacts). fix-visual-stability: self-generated 1.0 vs curated 0.0 on Claude Code because the creator wrote the pack inside the graded sandbox and listed the verifier test ids. Aggregate: -8.1 to -11.5 pp below no-skill on three configurations; Claude Code self-generated runs used effort max vs baseline high.
quote: Consumed packs lock in confident errors.
limits: Twelve hand-audited trajectories, not a statistical test. Creator sessions for the pre-baked family were not released; Gemini CLI trajectories omit tool outputs, so non-discovery is behavioural. The paper itself says the deficit mixes content quality, discovery and creator-solver interference.
agent_relevance: Self-written lessons do not fail for one reason. Fixes: write the lesson in a separate context from the solve, force the lesson into context instead of hoping it is found, and verify it on tasks the writer did not see (leakage guard).

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench v4, Appendix F.1 skill quantity and F.3 failure patterns
finding: Answers gap 7 partly. Benefit is flat from 1 to 3 skills per task and falls at 4 or more. The paper says overhead and conflicting guidance but did not separate those causes.
numbers: Table 8 (87 tasks, 18 configurations): 1 skill, 23 tasks, 32.2% to 50.2% (+18.0); 2-3 skills, 43 tasks, 34.4% to 53.4% (+19.0); 4+ skills, 21 tasks, 34.8% to 44.9% (+10.1). No-skill baselines are about equal across groups (32.2 to 34.8), so the drop is not simply harder tasks. Failure patterns on the 13 negative tasks: A heavyweight pipeline crowds out a simpler path; B skill displaces a stronger native strategy (exam-block-sequencing -7.4 pp, econ-detrending-correlation -5.6 pp); C skill points to a solver the agent cannot debug (suricata-custom-exfil -7.4 pp).
limits: Skill count is confounded with task type and total length; there was no length-matched control (the paper concedes this). Three trials per cell. The cause of the 4+ drop stays open: redundancy, conflict or context length each fit.
agent_relevance: Cap lessons per class at about 3, keep them short, add applicability limits and a fast fallback path. The remedy for pattern B is to say when not to use the lesson, which is the S0 gate in text form.

source: Cho and Park (2026) Skill Following: evaluating actual skill use in retrieval-enabled LLM agents (arXiv 2609.00549)
finding: Averages hide harm. When an agent chooses to fetch a skill, the same task done without the skill is often better, even when the headline retrieval lift is positive. The agent's own choice to retrieve is tied to task difficulty.
numbers: 17 LLMs, MBPP+, HumanEval+, Math500, paired skill-enabled vs skill-disabled runs with the same seed. Cells are aggregate lift / same-task effect (pp). MBPP+ seed 42: Gemini-2.5-Flash-lite +6.2 / -15.6; DeepSeek-V3.2 +31.6 / -9.1; Mistral-S-24B -27.2 / -22.5; Claude-4.5-H +1.4 / +1.4. Seed 44: DeepSeek-V3.2 +46.2 / -23.1. Math500: Llama-3.3-70B +14.2 aggregate vs -39.4 paired; Gemini-2.5-Flash-lite +13.2 vs -11.0. Controls (pooled paired effect, DeepSeek-V3.2 / Gemini-Flash-lite): normal -15.9 / -17.9; random skills -10.2 / -5.0; corrupted -15.1 / -15.4. The most frequent failure among 45 + 40 annotated harmful transitions was ignoring the retrieved skill.
limits: Small models, single seeds per cell with sign flips between seeds, skill library not curated for these tasks. Negative effect persists with random content, so part of it is the cost of the tool call or extra context, not bad lessons. Authors say the controls bound rather than identify the cause.
agent_relevance: Never judge lessons by comparing tasks where the agent asked for help against tasks where it did not: weak tasks self-select. Use paired on/off runs on the same item. This is the correct design for the S0 test.

source: Dong et al. (2026) Agent skills can be harmful: skill-induced failures in LLM agents (arXiv 2608.11888)
finding: Harmful skills are usually relevant ones, not irrelevant ones. They make the agent build the wrong thing, or do too much.
numbers: 307 confirmed skill-induced failures from SkillsBench and SWE-Skills-Bench using a differential method (run with skill vs run without, or with a matched skill): 125 functional failures and 182 efficiency regressions. Task-implementation fault 86 of 125 (68.8%); wrong artifact location 24 (19.2%); environment mismatch 13 (10.4%); applicability mismatch only 2 (1.6%). Efficiency: excessive procedure 114 of 182 (62.6%), of which excessive verification 67 and heavy pipelines 30; context bloat 46 (25.3%), and 43 of those 46 came from mandatory skill-body text.
limits: Failures were picked by the differential method, so this shows what harm looks like, not how often it happens. Reference runs are single runs and agent variance is a confound. I read the abstract, taxonomy and tables, not every case study.
agent_relevance: Applicability mismatch is tiny, so a relevance filter alone cannot fix harm. The lesson text itself must say what to skip. Gives an audit checklist: overlong procedures and mandatory checklists.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Break it down, pass it on: cross-task skill transfer in LLM agents (arXiv 2608.20274)
finding: Best cross-cell evidence yet for gap 1. Task-level lessons help mainly where the no-memory baseline is very low, and the benefit shrinks as the baseline rises. Subtask-level lessons stay above baseline.
numbers: 11 models, 3 benchmarks (AppWorld, OfficeBench, KramaBench), 33 model-benchmark cells, 95% task-bootstrap CIs. Across the 33 cells the task-level skill effect shrinks as the no-memory baseline rises: Spearman rho=-0.55 for text skills, -0.45 for code skills, both p<0.05. Examples (success %): Qwen3-235B on AppWorld none 7.4, task+text 18.0, task+code 14.4. GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld none 27.3, task+text 17.0, task+code 1.0 (69% of those code runs ended within two steps). Averages over 11 models and 3 benchmarks: task-level none 22.1, +text 20.9, +code 18.0; subtask-level none 24.8, +text 26.7, +code 25.3.
limits: Correlation across different models and benchmarks, not a within-model manipulation of competence. Baseline is confounded with model and benchmark. A clear sign flip shows only for task-level skills.
agent_relevance: The rho of about -0.5 is the first measured version of the S0 pattern in agents. A sign flip appears when lessons are task-specific and mismatched, not simply when the model is good. Store lessons at the subtask level.

source: Guo et al. (2026) SkillApt: learning when to reuse skills from execution feedback (arXiv 2609.26863)
finding: Relevance is not applicability. Deciding per state to load or skip a lesson, from paired with/without evidence, matches a strong zero-shot controller while loading far less. It also gives a count of how much evidence is enough.
numbers: Phase A: 20 skills, 160 held-out states. Cold start (never load) 81.9% task success; SkillApt 91.3% with activation 26.3% and 1,188.5 tokens; zero-shot LLM controller 91.3%, activation 98.8%, 1,811.7 tokens. Success plateau reached at about six evidence states per skill (12 was the pre-set endpoint; the curve is not monotone). Threshold sweep: 0.5 gives 91.3% at 26.3% activation; 0.6 gives 86.3% at 10.0% activation and 974.8 tokens. Phase B (199 tasks): no skill 81.4%, gold skill 83.4%, hard (top-ranked non-gold) candidate 78.4%; non-optimal skills mostly left correctness unchanged and raised cost. MedCalc-Bench with only 1 to 4 evidence pairs per skill: SkillApt never loaded; always-load 63/80 vs 73/80 without. A with-success-only history made the policy load almost everywhere (a skill was credited for 204 of its 227 successes).
limits: Small benchmark (20 skills, 160 states), single frozen executor, authors claim no causal guarantees. The zero-shot controller already gets the same success, so the gain is cost, not accuracy. Evidence collection needs paired runs (twice the compute).
agent_relevance: Template for S0: record a with/without pair on the same item, load only when the paired record shows net benefit, and expect about six pairs per class before the estimate settles. Success-only logging over-credits lessons.

source: Hu, Long and Wang (2026) When continual learning moves to memory: a study of experience reuse in LLM agents (arXiv 2604.27003)
finding: Within one model, test items were split by whether the no-memory agent already solved them. Mismatched stored experience hurt the unsolved items, not the solved ones. This is the reverse of an expertise-reversal prediction for the strong items.
numbers: ALFWorld and BabyAI, sequential tasks A then B. Raw trajectory memory, ALFWorld A to B: retention on baseline-success items RR=+4.6, new learning on baseline-fail items NL=-26.1 (pp). Raw forward transfer negative in both environments; abstract Insight memory turned it positive. Finer storage granularity helped in BabyAI A to B (+15.0 vs +9.0 aggregated) and not in the reverse direction (-1.0 vs +7.5).
limits: The memory came from a different task, so this tests relevance mismatch, not redundancy of a well-matched lesson. One model setup per environment. It does not test a matched lesson on items the agent already solves.
agent_relevance: On items the agent already passes, a lesson did no visible harm here; harm landed on hard items. A competence gate should mainly protect against mismatched lessons on weak items. Prefer abstract insights over raw trajectories.

source: Shang et al. (2026) When self-evolution backfires: pre-commit gating against skill contamination (VaG, arXiv 2608.05810)
finding: Bears on gaps 7 and 9 for self-written pools. With no gate, performance rises to a peak at a critical pool size and then falls back. Removing bad skills later recovers little, because later skills were written from them.
numbers: Terminal-Bench 2, five evolution rounds: ungated pass@1 peaks at round 3 and ends at round 5 only 2 points above round 1; VaG gated pool improves every round, reaches 72% pass@1 with a pool about 5 times smaller, 10 points above the ungated best round. Peak-to-R5 drop 12.3 pp; removing the source skills recovers 1.7 pp, oracle full-lineage cleanup 6.7 pp. Three mechanisms: single bad skill, harmless skills that conflict together, and systemic drift.
quote: past a critical pool size, newly added skills degrade performance instead of improving it
limits: Agent-written skills from its own trajectories, one benchmark for the main curve; gating uses three critics that cost extra calls. I read the abstract, introduction and result tables, not the full ablations.
agent_relevance: Cause of decline with count is a mix of defects and conflicts, not mere length. Test every new lesson before admission and cap the pool.

source: Cheng et al. (2026) Scope before you persist: preventing cross-family interference in agent memory (arXiv 2609.29144)
finding: Bears on gap 1 (scope of a lesson) from another angle. A lesson tested on one task family hurts other families when applied everywhere. Restricting each lesson to its own family removes the harm and keeps the gains.
numbers: PROCSTREAM-RSI, 12-round code-repair stream, frozen model. Global memory: mean hidden trajectory utility 0.713, below the static no-edit agent at 0.775, harmful deployments in 6 of 8. Same accepted skills retrieved only for the originating family: 0.816, harmful deployments 0 of 8. Over 27 paired randomised streams, Scoped-ORC beat Global-ORC by 0.063 [0.037, 0.094], accepted 63 vs 12 updates, 0 of 63 accepted updates harmful.
limits: Synthetic procedural stream with fixed oracle semantics; the authors say static performance of 0.775 reflects substantial prior competence and that the benchmark measures familiar contracts, not new semantics. Family labels are given, not inferred.
agent_relevance: Gate lessons by task-class label, as S0 already proposes. The saving came from scoping, not from a similarity threshold. A wrong class label would mean a wrong lesson.

source: Giampieri (2026) Cortex: measurement-gated evolution and pruning of coding-agent skills and rules (arXiv 2610.14216)
finding: Same-lesson, two-model result for gap 1, and a working model of fading (gap 4) by pruning. The same harness gained 66.7 points on the weaker model and 5.6 on a stronger model that already followed most conventions. A prune pass after the upgrade flagged half the items as removable.
numbers: Harness evolved with Claude Haiku 4.5, run R1: +66.7 points under Haiku 4.5; the same harness +5.6 points (95% CI [-2.8, +13.9]) under Claude Sonnet 5. One prune pass after the upgrade ran each item's tasks 3 times with and 3 times without: 2 of 4 items flagged removable. A skill listed on every turn was listed in 198 attempts and opened in none; rules that load automatically did most of the work. Deliberately useless and harmful suggestions: none kept, but harmful rules were tested on tasks that mostly failed anyway, so no verdict was reached. On a real open-source project where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn.
limits: Single repository built for the test, one run per harness, tiny task counts, a script played the developer, CI includes zero. The comparison is across two different models, not a cut inside one model's own per-class competence. The tool has one developer.
agent_relevance: A lesson's value shrinks as the solver gets better, with a CI that crosses zero rather than a clean reversal. Re-test lessons after any model change and prune those that no longer pay. Put important lessons where they load automatically, not where the agent must choose to open them.

source: Qiu et al. (2026) When correct demonstrations hurt, re-read for similarity and position (arXiv 2605.26350), Tables 2 and 3
finding: Bears on gap 3 (shift harm by model size). The perturbed examples that hurt small models were still very similar to the originals by cosine, so a similarity cut-off at usual levels would not have blocked them. Nothing in the paper tests a filter.
numbers: Table 2 original-vs-perturbed cosine similarity: SST-2 0.919; other splits 0.859 to 0.965 (Problemathic complex 0.859 with Jaccard overlap 0.683). Despite 0.919 cosine on SST-2, Llama-2-7B fell from 96.4 zero-shot to 56.9 at 100% perturbation. Table 3, SST-2 replacing 16/24/28 exemplars: Llama-2-7B random 94.7/88.2/72.9, tail 92.3/77.6/58.1; Llama-3.1-8B random 96.9/94.9/88.6; Qwen2.5-3B random 98.2/95.0/93.1. Attention maps: the 70B model re-weights to early clean exemplars; the 7B model attends to recent ones.
limits: Similarity measured between original and perturbed exemplars, not between exemplar and query. No retrieval filter was run. Harm is on small models; 70B-class models stayed near zero-shot. Perturbations were synthetic (irrelevant sentences or numbers added).
agent_relevance: A cosine threshold is not enough to stop shifted examples (0.92 similarity still hurt). Use outcome-checked scoping (d13) and put the most relevant lesson last, near the query (recency effect on small models). A direct test of a similarity gate is still missing.

source: Zhao et al. (2026) Coalition-aware skill reliability for self-evolving agents (arXiv 2608.22610)
finding: Skill value depends on the other skills in the bank and on the target domain. Bank-level gains hide skills with negative contributions, and skills that help at the source can reverse at the target.
numbers: Audit on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, HotpotQA, ALFWorld finds coalition pollution (accept/reject margins of 0.006 to 0.02 are only a few per-stage standard errors) and cross-domain utility reversal. Methods CASS (sampled Shapley marginals) and u-SMCO (mask transferred skills using unlabelled target data) are reported to beat skill-based baselines; sizes not verified.
limits: Only the abstract and the audit and definition sections were read, not the result tables.
agent_relevance: Treat a lesson as a property of (lesson, bank, domain). Test with and without in the target class, not only where it was written.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, Table 2 re-analysed for base-rate dependence (cross-check gaps 1, 3, 10)
finding: Across 18 model-harness configurations the size of the skill lift is unrelated to the no-skill pass rate. There is no model-level reversal in this data.
numbers: Computed from Table 2 (opened): Pearson r between no-skill pass and gain = -0.03; Spearman = -0.09; N = 18 configs, 87 tasks x 3 trials. No-skill range 16.0 to 51.5; gain range +4.1 to +25.7 pp. Low-gain strong starts: Gemini 3.5 Flash 41.1 to 48.2 (+7.1); Opus 4.8 45.7 to 54.1 (+8.4). High-gain strong starts: Codex GPT-5.5 46.8 to 66.5 (+19.7). Weakest start Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite 16.0 to 20.1 (+4.1).
quote: high base capability does not imply high Skill leverage
limits: The correlation is my own calculation from the published table, not a reported statistic. Configs mix harness and model. Curated skills, not agent-written. Pooled task set, not a within-class split.
agent_relevance: Base capability alone does not predict who benefits. A gate keyed to class pass rate cannot be justified from model-level data; it must be tested within class (compare d09, where agent-written lessons do fall with baseline).

source: Lin et al. (2026) Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit, SWE-bench Verified (gaps 3, 10)
finding: Benefit from an evolved harness (memory, skills, prompts) rises then falls with base pass rate. Mid models gain most; strong models gain little; the weakest gain less than mid.
numbers: SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks), base pass then best gain over three evolvers (pp): Qwen3-32B 3.6, +4.4; Qwen3-235B 20.7, +19.3; GPT-OSS-120B 26.2, +15.8; Haiku 4.5 66.0, +2.4; Sonnet 4.6 73.2, +2.8; Opus 4.6 74.2, +2.6.
quote: harness-benefit is non-monotonic in base capability
limits: The harness is a whole evolved bundle, not lessons or examples alone. Gain is the maximum over three evolvers, so biased upward. Preprint, 7 models, 3 benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Best fixed-task curve found for 'stronger model, less benefit'. It shows a ceiling at the top and a collapse at the bottom, so S0 needs a floor as well as a ceiling.

source: Lin et al. (2026) Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit, MCP-Atlas and SkillsBench (gap 3)
finding: The hump is weaker on two more benchmarks, and the SkillsBench cells are tiny.
numbers: MCP-Atlas (500 tasks), base then gain: Qwen3-32B 3.6, +1.0; Qwen3-235B 25.0, +4.3; GPT-OSS-120B 28.0, +7.0; Haiku 42.4, +3.6; Sonnet 54.0, +3.2; Opus 61.0, +3.6. SkillsBench (86 tasks): Qwen3-32B 0.0, +5.8; Qwen3-235B 4.7, +1.1; GPT-OSS 0.0, +7.0; Haiku 5.8, +15.1; Sonnet 24.4, +3.5; Opus 25.6, +5.8.
limits: On SkillsBench one task is about 1.2 pp and several bases are near 0, so the pattern is not clear there. Table columns were parsed from PDF layout and checked against the appendix matrix.
agent_relevance: Do not generalise the hump from one benchmark. Where the threshold sits (floor or ceiling) must be measured per model.

source: Lin et al. (2026) Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit, activation and adherence (gap 3)
finding: Weak models gain little because they often do not load the skill and, when they do, do not follow it. This is a limit on using a lesson, separate from redundancy.
numbers: SkillsBench skill-load rate / harness-following rate / pass-when-loaded: Qwen3-32B 0.251 / 0.142 / 0.023; GPT-OSS-120B 0.446 / 0.442 / 0.040; Haiku 4.5 0.794 / 0.600 / 0.099; Qwen3-235B 0.961 / 0.350 / 0.022; Sonnet 4.6 0.959 / 0.730 / 0.145; Opus 4.6 0.957 / 0.757 / 0.177. Weak-model adherence drifts 0.52 to 0.13 over a trajectory, over four times steeper than strong models.
limits: Following is judged by an LLM judge. Pass-when-loaded is low for all models, so it is conditional on hard tasks. One benchmark.
agent_relevance: A lesson shown to a very weak class may be dead weight. Rule 'show lessons only on weak classes' needs a floor. Repeat the lesson near its point of use in long tasks.

source: Lin et al. (2026) Harness Updating Is Not Harness Benefit, evolver side (gap 9)
finding: Harness updates written from execution evidence give gains almost independent of the strength of the model that writes them. These are not blind self-written skills.
numbers: Across evolvers, post-evolution score differs by at most 3.1 pp on any benchmark. A Qwen3.5-9B evolver gives gains comparable to Claude Opus 4.6. Strong agent with its worst evolver still leads the weakest agent with its best evolver by 18.6 to 35.2 pp.
limits: The evolver sees traces and feedback, unlike the SkillsBench self-generated arm that wrote skills before the task. No arm compares verified-failure lessons with ungrounded lessons at equal tokens, so the contrast is indirect.
agent_relevance: Supports writing lessons from observed, verified failures. Writer strength matters little; reader strength matters.

source: Feng et al. (2026) Cross-Task Skill Transfer, difficulty strata and early-stop failure (gaps 1, 6)
finding: Subtask-level skills fell below baseline in only two difficulty strata, both with intervals that include zero. Whole-task code skills can wreck an agent by making it stop early.
numbers: Subtask+Text below no-memory in OfficeBench easy (-1.9) and KramaBench hard (-0.4), both paired 95% CIs cover zero. GPT-OSS-120B on AppWorld with task-level code skills: 27.3 to 1.0; in 69% of those tasks it ended within 2 steps vs 0.2% with no memory. 75% to 83% of induced skills came from unsolved source tasks.
limits: Difficulty labels are benchmark annotations (or number of apps), not counts of interacting steps. Skills are induced online with no outcome gate.
agent_relevance: Item-level difficulty strata exist in public data, so the element-interactivity idea (gap 6) could be tested by a re-cut. A reused whole-task lesson can short-circuit the agent.

source: Liu et al. (2026) How Well Do Agentic Skills Work in the Wild (gaps 3, 10)
finding: With only generic retrieved skills, weaker models fall to or just below their no-skill score, while the stronger model gains a little.
numbers: 84 SkillsBench tasks x 3 runs. Claude: force-loaded 55.4, curated 51.2, with distractors 43.5, retrieved 40.1, no curated skills in pool 38.4 (3.0 above no skill). Kimi 19.8 vs 21.8 no skill. Qwen 19.7 vs 20.5 no skill. Kimi loads skills in 86% of runs but scores 38.9 curated vs 38.5 force-loaded.
quote: stronger models can better ignore irrelevant skills, while weaker models are more likely to be hurt
limits: Gaps of 0.8 to 2.0 pp on 84 tasks are inside noise. Model, harness and retrieval pipeline are confounded.
agent_relevance: Misapplied lessons cost something for weak readers; relevance checks matter more than quantity.

source: Ying et al. (2026) OpenSkillEval (gaps 3, 4)
finding: Strong agents consult skills selectively. Forcing a read raises use, but agents still skip or contradict steps.
numbers: Default: skill file read in about 48% of cases (100 instances per agent); Claude Opus 4.6 about 20%. With a force-use instruction the read rate rises to 94% and first read moves from step 4.4 to 3.3. 600+ generated tasks, 30 skills, 10 models.
limits: Read rate is not accuracy. Tasks are slides, posters, charts and reports scored by rubric. Preprint.
agent_relevance: A strong model already decides when a lesson is worth reading. Making lesson access optional (a tool call) may gate more cheaply than always putting it in the prompt.

source: Own calculation for gap 2: probe size and class pass rate
finding: With 3 to 5 probe items a class pass rate cannot place a class in a band reliably. About 20 or more items are needed for an interval narrower than plus or minus 0.2.
limits: Binomial, independent items, one attempt per item. Repeating one item gives less information than new items. A calculation run in this session (Python), not a literature result; no agent study of probe size was found.
agent_relevance: Use a smoothed estimate (prior from similar classes plus running count) and a wide middle band. A class with 3 items defaults to the middle band. Compare d10 (SkillApt plateau at about six paired states per skill).

source: Own calculation for gap 1: trials needed for a within-class lesson test
finding: Detecting a 5 pp lesson effect needs hundreds to a few thousand unpaired trials per arm. A 10 pp effect needs about 140 to 390.
numbers: Normal approximation, two-sided alpha 0.05, power 80%, unpaired arms. Baseline pass 0.5: 1568 per arm for 5 pp, 392 for 10 pp. Baseline 0.8: 1004 and 251. Baseline 0.9: 564 and 141. Xu and Wu could only detect 8.3 to 16.0 pp, consistent with this.
limits: A paired design (same items with and without the lesson, several seeds) needs fewer, by an amount that depends on unknown item-level correlation. A calculation run in this session, not a literature result.
agent_relevance: Plan the S0 test as paired, on items with zero-shot rate between 0.2 and 0.8, with 3 or more seeds per item. A 100-item test cannot answer a 5 pp question.

source: Tetzlaff et al. (2025) Table 3 re-derived: measured knowledge groups give a small reversal (gap 8)
finding: On the high-knowledge side, the reversal is large when groups differ by grade level and small when groups come from a median split on a knowledge test or from a short intervention. Our agent's band cut is closer to the second case.
numbers: Table 3 high-prior-knowledge estimates (dummy coded, reference = grade level -0.95, CI [-1.32, -0.58]): field of study -0.08 (p=.77), measurement +0.74 [0.34, 1.14] (p<.001), intervention +0.75 [0.22, 1.28] (p=.006), self-evaluation +0.16. Adding the offsets gives about -0.21 for measured groups (j=32, k=48) and about -0.20 for intervention groups (j=7, k=8). Authors: moderation for high-knowledge learners R2 = 50.00%. Low side: educational status R2 = 25.92%, content area R2 = 20.59%; humanities and language weak.
limits: Offsets added by me, assuming dummy coding as the table notes say; the paper states the reversal is weakest for measurement and intervention, which agrees in sign. Some cells have 2 to 8 studies. No moderator test for the difference of differences.
agent_relevance: Expect only about -0.2 on the expert side when bands come from a measured pass rate. A lesson gate on a measured class pass rate is the weak-effect case, so plan for a small effect and a paired design.

source: Xu and Wu (2026) Skill Availability and Presentation Granularity, re-check (gaps 1, 6)
finding: Re-read: 30 tasks (15 hard, 15 medium by repository metadata), two models, no split by measured per-task pass rate. It cannot test reversal by competence.
numbers: Worked example inside a skill: +0.7 and +1.3 pp, CIs include zero (K18). Tasks were stratified by designers' difficulty label only.
limits: Preprint. Trial-level data not checked.
agent_relevance: Re-cut by per-task no-skill pass rate if trial data are public, else rerun with the paired design in d26.

source: Kalyuga, Chandler and Sweller 1998, 2000; Kalyuga et al. 2001 primary papers (critique section 5, not a numbered gap)
finding: Not opened. The primary papers are paywalled and no open copy was found with the tools left (web search quota exhausted; OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv API returned 429). The founding numbers still rest on the 2007 review table (a03 to a05, b01 to b04).
numbers: No new numbers. Kalyuga 2007 review values stay: range 0.45 to 2.99, mid 1.72 (see K01).
limits: Still second-hand. The review says its effect sizes were computed conservatively; this could not be checked against variances, dropouts or test timing.
agent_relevance: Treat the 1998 to 2001 numbers as second-hand. Tetzlaff 2025 (difference 0.971) is the better anchor.

source: Search status for gaps 4, 5 and 6 in agents (negative result of this session)
finding: Within the sources opened, no agent study tests faded lessons that shrink as pass rate rises, a name-the-principle line for far transfer, delayed or held-out reversal on the same items, or a per-class competence signal compared across methods. The few arXiv listing queries that ran returned nothing matching. This gap-search pass found no additional study that tests expertise reversal of lessons for a language-model agent with a within-class competence split.
numbers: arXiv listing query 'expertise reversal': 1 result (He-Yueya 2024, 2403.02795). 'worked examples fading LLM': 0 results. The web search quota ran out partway; later OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and arXiv listing calls returned 429.
limits: Absence of evidence under a limited search, not proof that no study exists.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4, 5 and 6 remain open for agents. Partial pointers: d14 (pruning after a model change is a form of fading), d09 and d13 (task streams with held-out later tasks), d22 (difficulty strata), d27 (measured groups give a small effect).
